issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

vignette:
Earl had spent most of his life making a living by knowing streets, schedules, and people's habits, so when the assault happened on an ordinary afternoon run, it struck him not only as an attack but as a collapse of the rules he had relied on. He was unloading packages outside a small row of shops when a man came up fast, demanded his wallet, and shoved him hard enough that Earl hit the side of the truck and went down awkwardly on one knee. The man was gone within moments, but Earl remembered the metallic taste in his mouth, the humiliation of being pinned there in public, and the shocked realization that he had not seen it coming. In the weeks afterward, he kept returning to that moment and to the thought that he should have done something different, some better choice, some quicker move; he could not trust that he would do the right thing if he were ever put on the spot again. More than the bruise or the fear, what stayed with him was the sense that the world no longer worked the way it once had. A stranger on a sidewalk, a routine delivery, even daylight in a busy commercial strip now felt proof that the basic order of things had been shattered.

As those beliefs settled in, Earl began organizing his days around keeping himself from having to sit with them. He worked hard at keeping busy, volunteering for extra errands, filling gaps with household repairs, yard work, and long drives that gave him something to do with his hands and a reason not to be alone with his thoughts. At home, when the memory of the assault pressed in, he tried hard not to think about the event at all, cutting off the image of the man's face or the feel of the pavement under his knee before it could fully form. He found that if he let himself dwell on it, he would be overwhelmed, and that conviction made avoidance feel like the safest option. Even his eating changed in the service of that effort: he began overeating at night, standing in the kitchen after dinner and reaching for snacks or leftovers in a way that dulled the tension for a while and gave him a different sensation to focus on. His wife noticed that he was always in motion and always headed for the pantry, but Earl experienced these habits as necessary discipline, the only way he could keep himself from tipping into something he feared he would not manage.

The trouble was that the more he organized himself around not thinking, the more the assault seemed to define what kind of man he believed himself to be. Earl had once prided himself on being careful, dependable, and capable, yet the assault left him doubting that he could trust his own judgment in a crisis. That self-doubt made every outside errand feel loaded, especially the deliveries he still drove part-time, where he found himself scanning corners and parking lots with a tightness in his chest, half expecting another person to appear suddenly at arm's length. He did not say this to many people, but in the quiet after a shift he would admit to himself that his beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed, and that made even ordinary places feel less real, less safe, and less governable by common sense. He became more rigid in the routes he took and more eager to finish work quickly, not because the job itself had changed, but because being out in the world kept confirming the same frightening lesson.

Over time, these habits narrowed his life. The avoidance protected him from brief surges of distress, but it also kept the assault present in a muted, persistent way, as if there were no stable place left to put it. When he arrived for help, it was because his wife finally told him she missed the man who used to sit through dinner without disappearing into work, snacks, or silence, and because Earl was increasingly afraid that if he ever paused long enough to think about the assault, he truly would not be able to handle it. At 77, he did not want to spend whatever remained of his life organizing himself around one violent afternoon. What he hoped for was simple but urgent: to feel able to face the memory without being taken over by it, and to find out whether his judgment and the world he knew could be trusted again.
